title: POC scoping - Skyward AI - latency & throughput SLOs
summary: POC scoping focused on defining latency SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing and benchmark plan. Customer wants interactive chat SLOs and validation plan across warm/cold cache, networking, and model variants. Redwood to share benchmark harness, pricing/estimates, and security docs; Skyward to provide sample traces and test account for VPC peering. Agreement on timeline: initial bench in 2 weeks, pilot week in 4 weeks, acceptance criteria documented.
topics: p95/p99 SLOs and what they mean for UX
Workload sizing: QPS, concurrency, prompt/response lengths
Benchmark methodology: replay vs synthetic, warm vs cold cache
Measurement plan: client vs server metrics, instrumentation
transcript:
00:00 Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we've got about an hour set aside to nail down the SLOs and the measurement plan for the POC with Skyward. does that still work?
00:07 Lena: yes thanks Maya, we specifically want to validate interactive performance for our chat feature, and understand the tradeoffs between hosted and dedicated.
00:14 Ravi: awesome; quick intro - I'm Ravi, I run infra benchmarks on the SE team. today's goal is to align on TTFT vs TPOT, targets (p95/p99), sample workload, and how we'll measure.
00:25 Omar: hi, Omar here. for context our current infra is k8s on GCP, most traffic goes through a regional LB, avg RTT to our app is ~18ms.
00:34 Priya: and our typical prompt length is 120 tokens; we expect responses around 80 tokens for the chat use-case.
00:42 Tom: product is aiming for a human-like interactive experience - sub-second feel for first reply so customers don't notice lag.
00:50 Maya: ok great, let's define terms first. TTFT (time-to-first-token) is time from request arrival at the server to first generated token leaving the server; TPOT is time-per-output-token after the first token - so basically slope of token emission. those are the two SLO primitives we'll use.
01:05 Priya: that matches our understanding. question: do you include network time in TTFT?
01:10 Ravi: good point. we typically provide both server-side TTFT (service-side processing only) and end-to-end TTFT (client observed). SLOs should be specified both ways: customer-facing E2E and infra SLOs for root-causing.
01:22 Lena: ok, for product we care about E2E, but for engineering acceptance we'll need server-side numbers too.
01:28 Maya: suggested baseline targets for chat interactive experience: TTFT p95 < 200ms, p99 < 500ms; TPOT p95 < 20ms/token, p99 < 50ms/token for the model class you plan to use. these are starting points; we should adjust after you share sample logs.
01:44 Omar: that p95/p99 range seems reasonable. what's typical for larger models though? we're considering a 13B quantized model for accuracy.
01:52 Ravi: for a 13B on A100/RTX-class inference, warmed KV cache, TPOT often sits around 10-30ms/token depending on batch and sequence length; TTFT can be higher if cold-start or large context needs compilation - warm steady-state TTFT can be 80-200ms. quantization (4-bit/8-bit) helps reduce TPOT but sometimes increases variance.
02:10 Priya: we need concrete SLOs tied to our success criteria. product wants < 250ms first token 95% of the time in US regions and < 1s at p99.
02:19 Maya: ok let's capture that as customer-facing acceptance criteria. engineering acceptance criteria will be server TTFT p95 < 180ms, p99 < 450ms; TPOT p95 < 25ms/token, p99 < 60ms/token.
02:31 Tom: how do you measure TPOT for multi-token streaming? do you use the average inter-token delta?
02:36 Ravi: yes we measure per-response inter-token deltas and build latency histograms per-token offset (e.g., tokens 1-16, 17-64). we also report slope (ms/token) and variance. and we separate first-chunk generation (first 1-8 tokens) from steady emission.
02:52 Maya: important note: user experience depends heavily on TTFT (perceived latency) and then on TPOT for longer responses. so for short replies TTFT dominates. for longer replies both matter.
03:03 Priya: on workload sizing - projected peak QPS is 120 requests/s, 95th expected concurrency ~220 concurrent requests; average prompt 120 tokens, avg response 80 tokens. does that change suggestions?
03:15 Ravi: that's helpful. with 120 QPS and 220 concurrency you need to size for burst capacity. Redwood recommended configuration is to reserve enough vCPU/GPU capacity to sustain p95 latency at 1.5x expected concurrency, plus autoscale for bursts. we'll include batching policies to maintain throughput without inflating TTFT too much.
03:31 Omar: can you explain batching tradeoffs? we've seen batching reduce cost but spike first-token wait.
03:36 Ravi: yep tradeoff: larger batch sizes improve throughput (lower TPOT and cost/token) but increase TTFT because the runtime waits to fill batch or to the max batching delay. Redwood's runtime has adaptive batching that attempts low-latency thresholds and priority lanes for interactive traffic. for the POC we'll test a few batching configs: low-latency (max batch 8, max wait 8ms) and throughput (max batch 64, max wait 25ms).
03:56 Lena: good - we want both configs tested.
04:00 Tom: benchmarks - what harness do you use? replaying live traffic or synthetic?
04:04 Maya: we recommend a two-pronged approach: 1) replay of anonymized production traces to hit realistic distributions (we'll need a sample trace from you), and 2) synthetic stress runs to map the latency envelope across QPS/concurrency/model variants. we'll share our harness (link in notes).
04:20 Priya: how do you handle KV cache that depends on prefix reuse? our customers have a lot of shared prefixes in flows.
04:26 Ravi: we'll include scenarios: cold-cache (no prefix reuse), warm-cache (steady reuse), and KV-primed (pre-warm cache with synthetic warmup). measurement plan explicitly separates these. caching can drastically reduce TTFT on common prompts.
04:40 Maya: measurement plan details: we will run baseline server-side microbenchmarks (TTFT/TPOT histograms), end-to-end runs from your app region to Redwood endpoints, and a replay week where we run your traces through the harness. we'll produce dashboards with p50/p95/p99 and token-slice views.
04:57 Omar: instrumentation - what do you need from our side to get accurate E2E numbers?
05:02 Ravi: we'll need a lightweight client-side tracer or network pings during tests. ideally you can run a container in your VPC to hit Redwood endpoints (VPC peering or private endpoint) so we can separate internet variance. if not, we at least need annotated samples of upstream app-to-redwood RTTs.
05:17 Lena: security concerns - we'll need SOC2 details, encryption, KMS, and a narrow scope for the POC.
05:23 Maya: we'll send the security packet and a short SOC2 summary doc; for POC we can do a short-term isolated project with token rotations. link: https://redwood.example.com/security/skyward-poc-packet
05:32 Tom: acceptance criteria recap?
05:35 Maya: customer-facing acceptance: E2E TTFT p95 < 250ms, p99 < 1s across US region; E2E TPOT p95 < 30ms/token. engineering acceptance: server-side TTFT p95 < 180ms, p99 < 450ms; TPOT p95 < 25ms/token, p99 < 60ms/token. success also requires stable throughput at peak expected QPS (120 QPS) with less than 5% error rate and resource usage within cost thresholds we'll provide.
05:58 Priya: what's the POC timeline?
06:01 Maya: proposed timeline: week 0 (this week) - onboarding + exchange traces + access; week 1 - bench harness setup and initial microbenchmarks; week 2 - replay runs and network-separated E2E runs; week 3 - pilot week at target QPS with two model configs and batching variants; week 4 - final report and acceptance decision. so about 4 weeks to acceptance.
06:21 Omar: that timeline fits our Q4 planning. what about cost/estimates?
06:26 Maya: we'll send an initial estimate after we pick model variants. we'll include cost sensitivity to batch sizes and quantization.
06:33 Tom: instrumentation and dashboards - will we get prometheus/trace endpoints?
06:37 Ravi: Redwood provides detailed dashboards per-route and model, plus traces for slow requests and token-level histograms. we can also push metrics to your prometheus if you prefer.
06:47 Lena: anything else on measurement specifics?
06:49 Priya: yes clarify how you handle cold starts - container spin-up versus model compilation.
06:53 Ravi: we'll measure cold-start separately: cold container start (minutes) is not in the normal SLO; cold-model compile (first request is slower due to kernel compilation) is measured and we'll report cold / warm delta. POC acceptance is based on warm-state SLOs but we'll document cold behavior.
07:08 Maya: ok let's go through action items and next steps.
07:11 Tom: quick note: speaker 6 cut in earlier, we didn't catch name - that's our infra ops, will send contact in slack.
07:18 Maya: thanks, please send.
07:20 Maya: end transcript.

Redwood (Maya) - Send security packet & SOC2 summary - due 2027-09-15
